chunks: Typical inductor core materials. The question: What are typical core materials?
Inductor cores come in several materials, and each one is good at a different job. The main ones are ferrite, powdered iron, silicon steel, and nanocrystalline alloys.
The answer is a short match-up: which material fits which frequency and current. You choose by how much magnetic flux it can hold, how much energy it wastes, and its cost.
Think of choosing a vehicle. A sports car is fast but carries little. A truck carries a lot but is slow. A van sits in between.
Core materials are the same: ferrite is the sports car (fast at high frequency, small load capacity), silicon steel is the truck (high capacity, only low frequency), and powder cores are the van.
The comparison simplifies one thing: every material also has a cost and temperature behavior.
Approximate regions (illustrative; grades vary).
Metals (powder, steel, nanocrystalline) reach high B sat (energy per volume), ferrites trade low B sat for high resistivity and low high-frequency loss.
Powder cores sit at low micro because their distributed gaps dilute the permeability.
Permeability: how strongly the material concentrates magnetic flux. Saturation flux density ( B sat ): the most flux the material can carry.
Core loss: energy wasted as heat in the core, which rises with frequency. Ferrite: a ceramic of iron oxide. It is an insulator, so it has low loss at high frequency.
Powder core: metal particles in a binder, which saturate gradually.
You need an inductor for a buck converter (a power supply that switches on and off 500,000 times a second to step a voltage down). It carries a large steady (DC) current.
A ferrite core has low loss at 500 kilohertz but saturates hard, so you add an air gap. A powdered-iron core saturates softly and handles DC well.
You pick the powder core, or a gapped ferrite. That is the whole idea.
"The main core materials are ferrite, powdered iron and its relatives like sendust and MPP, laminated silicon steel, and amorphous or nanocrystalline alloys.
Ferrite is low loss for tens of kHz to a few MHz but saturates hard around 0. 3 to 0. 5 tesla.
Powder cores have distributed gaps, so low permeability, around 1 tesla, and soft saturation, which suits DC-biased power inductors. Silicon steel is for line frequency.
Nanocrystalline is for common-mode chokes."
